title: Driver architecture and API contracts
source_notes:
Use this when you must choose how a driver hands items back to the sequence. The invariant is that sequence acceptance, physical bus completion, and response routing are three separate obligations. Templates 02 to 04 implement the three choices.

**Interview answer.** "I first decide whether the sequence must wait for bus completion. If yes, I use a serialized driver. If not, I decouple acceptance from execution with an owned queue. If the protocol has independent channels or multiple outstanding transactions, I run one worker thread per channel and track outstanding work by ID."

The three choices:

- **Serialized completion.** One transaction finishes on the interface before the next starts (Template 02).

- **Decoupled request and response.** The sequence is released early while the driver finishes the transfer (Template 03).

- **Independent channels.** Separate threads drive concurrent channels such as AXI AW and W, with several transactions in flight (Template 04).

**Rules to quote.**

- `get_next_item()` needs exactly one `item_done()`.

- `get()` finishes the sequencer handshake itself. Never call `item_done()` after it.

- Calling `item_done()` early releases the sequence. It does not pipeline the bus. Pipelining needs independent protocol threads.

- Copy routing IDs into every response with `rsp.set_id_info(req)`, or the response goes to the wrong sequence.

- Only one thread may write a given pin. A reset process that also drives pins needs an explicit arbiter.

- AXI4-Lite has no transaction IDs, so responses complete in order. ID-based matching applies to full AXI4.

**Practice.**

- Q249 Component Hierarchy and Driver-Sequencer Handshake

title: Serialized pull driver and reset ownership
Decoupled driver with an owned request queue
Independent channels, multiple outstanding transactions, and AXI rules
source_notes:
Use this when channels progress independently or several requests can be in flight. The invariant is that tracking state is registered before any response can arrive, and each transaction and credit is retired exactly once.

**Interview answer.** "For an AXI write I fork the AW and W handshakes because either may finish first, then wait for B. For multiple outstanding transactions I split the driver into an acceptor, an issue worker, and a response worker. The issue worker records the transaction by ID before it drives the request, so an early response always finds its entry."

```systemverilog
task drive_one_write(bus_req req, bus_rsp rsp);
  fork
    drive_aw_until_handshake(req);
    drive_w_until_handshake(req);
  join
  collect_b_response(rsp);
endtask
```

Multi-outstanding algorithm:

```text
acceptor:
    reserve one outstanding credit
    get request, clone it, keep routing IDs
    release the sequencer handshake
    enqueue the clone for the issue worker

issue worker:
    allocate a free protocol ID (if the protocol has IDs)
    record the pending entry BEFORE a response can appear
    drive the request until its handshake completes
    record issue time

response worker:
    observe the response handshake
    find the pending entry by ID, or by order if there are no IDs
    reject unknown, duplicate, stale, or early responses
    collect data beats until the last beat
    build the UVM response with the saved routing IDs
    retire the entry and free the ID and credit

reset owner:
    stop accepting new requests
    abort every queued and in-flight entry exactly once
    reconcile credits and scoreboard expectations
    resume after reset is released
```

**Choosing the tracking structure.**

- In-order completion: one FIFO queue for reads and one for writes.

- At most one active transaction per ID: associative array `pending[id]`.

- Several active transactions with the same ID: a FIFO queue per ID.

- Bursts: keep a beat counter next to each handle.

**AXI 4KB boundary rule (Q114).** An AXI burst must not cross a 4KB address boundary. 4KB is the smallest address region a slave or memory page can own, so a crossing burst could hit two slaves while the interconnect decodes only the first address. WRAP bursts never cross because they are aligned to their total size (at most 16 beats of 128 bytes, 2KB). FIXED bursts do not increment. Only INCR bursts need the check.

```systemverilog
// Stimulus: keep INCR bursts inside one 4KB page
constraint no_4k_cross_c {
  (burst == INCR) ->
    (((int'(addr[11:0]) >> size) << size) + ((int'(len) + 1) << size)) <= 4096;
}

// Checker on the AW channel
function automatic bit crosses_4k(logic [31:0] a, logic [7:0] len, logic [2:0] size);
  int unsigned first = (int'(a[11:0]) >> size) << size;
  return (first + ((int'(len) + 1) << size)) > 4096;
endfunction

ap_4k: assert property (@(posedge aclk) disable iff (!aresetn)
  awvalid && awburst == 2'b01 |-> !crosses_4k(awaddr, awlen, awsize));
```

Worked case: `addr=0xFF0, size=2 (4 bytes), len=3` gives 4 beats ending at byte 0xFFF, which is legal. `len=4` adds a beat at 0x1000 and crosses.

**Valid/ready handshake (Q65).** A transfer happens on a clock edge where `valid && ready`. The source must not wait for `ready` before asserting `valid`, and once `valid` is high it stays high with stable payload until the transfer. The destination may wait for `valid` before asserting `ready`.

**Packet stream signals (Q72).** A stream interface needs `valid`, `ready`, `data`, an end-of-packet marker (`last`), byte enables or an empty count for the final beat (`keep`), and often a sideband (`user`) and error flag. AXI4-Stream uses TVALID, TREADY, TDATA, TKEEP, TLAST, TUSER.

**Stress cases.** AW before W, W before AW, long backpressure, a reused ID, a response in the same cycle as issue, reset in the middle of a burst, a missing or extra `WLAST`/`RLAST`.

title: Shared contract for the APB example
source_notes:
Templates 06 to 13 build one connected APB testbench. Every component must agree on what counts as accepted, what reset cancels, and when the test is complete. Interviewers often ask you to state this contract before you write any code.

**Interview answer.** "Before coding I fix the contract. The target is APB4 with 32-bit aligned word accesses and byte strobes. It behaves like plain memory, errors change nothing, and reset clears everything the model knows. The driver drives on the falling edge, and the monitor samples on the rising edge."

**DUT contract.** One APB4 target. 32-bit byte addresses and data, word-aligned. Four byte strobes. PPROT tied to zero. The target behaves like plain memory. A successful write changes only enabled bytes. A successful read returns the stored bytes. An error response changes nothing. Reset clears the model. The smoke test writes every byte before reading it.

**Timing contract.** The driver drives on the falling edge. The monitor samples on the rising edge with `#1step` input skew. Request signals stay stable through the accepting rising edge. Reset is sampled on a rising edge, so the driver cancels on the next clock instead of clearing pins asynchronously. A separate test watchdog catches a stopped clock or a stuck transfer.

**APB facts.** A transfer is a setup phase followed by one or more access cycles. PREADY low extends access, and request signals hold steady while it is low. PSLVERR is valid only in the cycle where PSEL, PENABLE, and PREADY are all high (Arm IHI 0024D).

**How the pieces connect.** 06 defines `apb_if`. 07 defines `apb_item`. 08 drives items onto the interface. 09 creates scenarios and consumes responses. 10 turns pin activity into transactions. 11 predicts and checks memory contents. 13 builds the environment and ends the test. Template 12 is the general matching method for other DUTs. The APB scoreboard does not depend on it.

**Build order.** Compile the interface first. Then compile one package that imports `uvm_pkg`, includes `uvm_macros.svh`, and contains the item, driver, sequences, monitor, scoreboard, environment, and test. The top module supplies the DUT, clock, reset, and `uvm_config_db` setup.

**Stress point.** A test can pass the driver's response checks while the monitor and scoreboard still find a mismatch. The driver's view of the bus is not independent evidence.

source_notes:
Use this when expected and actual transactions arrive on separate streams, possibly reordered. The invariant is that each completed operation matches exactly once, and anything left unmatched at end of test is an error.

**Interview answer.** "I key both sides on something the monitor can observe, such as port plus ID. Each key holds a FIFO on the expected side and a FIFO on the actual side, so the actual can arrive first. When both FIFOs for a key are non-empty I pop and compare. A watchdog flags entries older than the latency bound, and at end of test both tables must be empty."

**Choosing the structure.** Strict in-order: one expected FIFO and one actual FIFO. Reordering across IDs with in-order completion per ID: a queue per ID. Compute the key on both arrivals independently.

```text
key = (reset_epoch, source_port, protocol_id)
expected[key] and actual[key] are FIFO queues of copied transactions

on_expected(e):
    enqueue copy of e with its time
    match(key(e))
on_actual(a):
    enqueue copy of a with its time
    match(key(a))
match(k):
    while expected[k] and actual[k] are both non-empty:
        e = pop expected[k]; a = pop actual[k]
        compare only the fields the spec defines
        delete empty queues
periodic_watchdog(now):
    check every unmatched entry on BOTH sides
    fail any entry older than the latency bound
on_reset:
    report or cancel every outstanding entry
    flush queues, advance the epoch, resume
end_of_test (check_phase):
    both tables empty AND sent count == completed count
```

**Pipelined adder, strict order (Q204).** One queue. For unsigned 32-bit inputs with a 33-bit result, predict `{1'b0,a} + {1'b0,b}` only when the input is accepted. Pop the oldest prediction for each accepted output. Stall cycles create nothing.

**ID reordering (Q166, Q281).** A queue per ID works only if same-ID responses stay in order. If they do not, you need another observable key. Never invent a sequence number the monitor cannot see.

**Duplicates (Q222, Q271).** With a unique token per transaction, keep a set of retired tokens and fail on a repeat. With reusable IDs, the ID alone cannot tell a duplicate from a new transaction, so you need a rule from the spec. A leftover entry at timeout is not proof of a duplicate.

**Split and reassemble (Q280, Q285).** A 512-bit transaction over a 64-bit link is 8 beats. Track expected length, a received-beat bitmap, beat index, byte enables, and the last marker. Reject duplicate or out-of-range beats. Compare only after the packet is complete. Time out missing beats.

**Leading drop and garbage bits (Q268).** Define the alignment rule first, for example "the first valid byte follows the start marker". Then discard input before the marker in the model, not in the comparator.

**Adversarial traces.** The actual for key 7 arrives before its prediction, waits, then matches once. Two predictions share ID 3 and need two queue entries, not one overwritten array slot. An unmatched actual must fail end-of-test even when the expected table is empty.

title: Environment, configuration, phases, and test completion
Register model and memory verification
source_notes:
Use this when you separate register behavior from bus transport. The invariant is that bus activity, the DUT's real state, and the register model must agree under each field's access policy.

**Interview answer.** "The register model mirrors the DUT's registers. A frontdoor access goes through the adapter and the real bus, so it tests address decode. A backdoor access reads or writes the HDL path directly, with no bus cycles. A predictor updates the mirror from monitored bus traffic. I compare frontdoor and backdoor results to catch decode bugs and aliasing."

**Method.**

- An adapter converts `uvm_reg_bus_op` to bus items with `reg2bus` and back with `bus2reg`.

- Give every field an access policy: RO, WO, RW, W1C, RC, and so on.

- Use frontdoor accesses to test decode and backdoor accesses to inspect storage.

- Write a unique, address-dependent pattern to every location to expose aliasing.

**What happens on a register write (Q237).** `reg.write()` builds a `uvm_reg_bus_op`, the adapter converts it to a bus item, the item runs on the bus sequencer, the driver drives it, and the predictor (explicit or auto) updates the mirror.

**Write-only register testbench (Q230).** Reads return a defined value (often 0) or an error, so you cannot check by reading back. Check the register's effect instead, through the function it controls or a backdoor peek.

**Aliasing with frontdoor only (Q256).** Write a unique value to each register, then read all of them back. Two registers that return the same last-written value share storage.

**Memory swap bug (Q295).** Frontdoor-write a known pattern, backdoor-peek the storage. If address A's data lands in B's storage, the decode is swapped.

**Firmware writes enable but the device does not start (Q291).** Check in order: did the write reach the bus (monitor), was the address decoded (backdoor peek), is the field really RW, is there a lock or clock gate, and is the DUT in reset.

title: Verification planning and coverage closure
source_notes:
Use this when asked what to verify, how to observe it, and when you are done. The invariant is that each requirement has a stimulus, an automatic check, and a coverage goal.

**Interview answer.** "I start from the spec and list features. For each feature I write down how to stimulate it, what checks it automatically, and which coverage proves I exercised it. I call it done when every requirement is checked and covered, regressions are clean across seeds, and the remaining holes are either waived with a reason or proven unreachable."

| Requirement | Stimulus | Automated check | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Normal operation | Directed and constrained-random | Reference model comparison | Legal operation bins |
| Boundaries | Min, max, wrap, empty, full | Boundary assertions | Boundary and transition bins |
| Concurrency | Overlap, competing requests, stalls | Ordering and accounting checks | Targeted crosses |
| Error and reset | Error injection, reset mid-transfer | Specified recovery behavior | Error and recovery scenarios |

**Coverage below 100% (Q274).** Sort each hole into one of four causes: missing stimulus, behavior that is illegal or unreachable, an overconstrained generator, or a wrong coverage model. Each needs a different fix.

**Code vs functional coverage (Q213).** Code coverage (line, branch, condition, toggle, FSM) shows what RTL ran. Functional coverage shows which spec features you exercised. You need both, because 100% code coverage can still miss an unimplemented feature.

**Covergroup example (Q176, Q258).**

```systemverilog
covergroup cg_data @(posedge clk iff valid);
  cp_data: coverpoint data {
    bins zero     = {0};
    bins max      = {8'hff};
    bins low[4]   = {[1:127]};
    bins high[4]  = {[128:254]};
  }
  cp_op: coverpoint op;
  x_op_data: cross cp_op, cp_data;
endgroup
```

In UVM, put the covergroup in a `uvm_subscriber` connected to the monitor, and sample it in `write()`.

**Other frequent questions.**

- Formal verification (Q270) proves a property for all inputs within a bound, using assumptions to rule out illegal inputs. It is strongest for control logic and weak for large datapaths.

- Gate-level simulation (Q272) is still needed for reset and X behavior, timing-annotated paths, scan insertion, and synthesis assumptions that RTL simulation cannot see.

- Emulation (Q357) runs the RTL on dedicated hardware, thousands of times faster than simulation, with good debug visibility. FPGA prototyping is faster still but has less visibility and needs RTL changes to fit the FPGA.

- AI-generated code (Q294) must be reviewed like any other code, and its checks must be tested to show they can fail.

title: Failure triage and reproducibility
source_notes:
Use this to explain how you debug a mismatch, a hang, X propagation, or a failure you cannot reproduce. The invariant is to find the earliest point of divergence, not the last symptom.

**Interview answer.** "I reproduce with the same seed, build, and options. Then I find the first transaction where the DUT and the model disagree, and decide whether the DUT, the monitor, or the model is wrong. After the fix I add a regression test that hits that case."

**Method.**

1. Record seed, test name, simulator version, options, and source revision.

2. Reproduce, then shrink the stimulus.

3. Compare failing and passing runs at transaction boundaries.

4. Decide which is wrong: DUT, monitor sampling, or reference model.

5. Fix the cause and add a targeted test.

**Hang (Q265).** Check which objections are still raised (`+UVM_OBJECTION_TRACE`), which threads are blocked, which bus transfers are pending, and which scoreboard queues are non-empty. Common causes are a missing `item_done`, a `wait` on an event that already fired, and a zero-delay loop.

**Cannot reproduce (Q266).** Different build, different seed source, a race between processes, or uninitialized state.

**X sources (Q267).** Uninitialized registers and memories, multiple drivers, undriven inputs, out-of-range array reads, X from power-down domains, and `case` without a default.

**Multiple CPUs read inconsistent data (Q22).** Suspect coherence: a missing invalidation, a write-back that has not completed, or a missing memory barrier. Trace the line's coherence state per core (Template 34).

**Stress cases.** The DUT is right but the monitor sampled the wrong cycle. The model ignores byte enables. The same seed produces different results on a different build.

title: Constraints: domains, relations, sums, and overrides
Intervals, allocation, and alignment
source_notes:
Use this for address regions, excluded ranges, or allocators. The invariant is to represent every region as half-open `[start, end)`, which makes adjacency and overlap tests simple.

**Interview answer.** "I store each region as start plus length and compute end in a wider type so it cannot wrap. Two regions do not overlap when one ends at or before the other starts. Alignment is `start % align == 0`."

```text
end = start + length          // widen before adding
start % alignment == 0
no_overlap(i, j) = end_i <= start_j  OR  end_j <= start_i
```

```systemverilog
rand bit [31:0] start[N];
rand bit [31:0] len[N];
constraint regions_c {
  foreach (start[i]) {
    len[i] inside {[1:256]};
    start[i] % 32 == 0;
    longint'(start[i]) + len[i] <= 1024;
  }
  foreach (start[i]) foreach (start[j])
    if (i < j) (longint'(start[i]) + len[i] <= start[j]) ||
               (longint'(start[j]) + len[j] <= start[i]);
}
```

**Bitmask alignment.** `(start & (align - 1)) == 0` works only for power-of-two alignment. For alignment 6, address 8 passes the mask test but fails modulo.

**Excluded range (Q128).** `!(addr inside {[EX_LO:EX_HI]});`

**Repeated randomization until full (Q129).** Keep a list of allocated regions in the class and constrain each new region against all of them. Stop when randomization fails or the space is full.

**2D rectangles (Q123).** Two rectangles do not overlap when one is completely left, right, above, or below the other: `x1+w1 <= x2 || x2+w2 <= x1 || y1+h1 <= y2 || y2+h2 <= y1`.

**Stress cases.** Zero length, a region that fills the space exactly, wraparound at the top address, and adjacent regions that touch but do not overlap. Template 07 applies this to DMA descriptors.

title: Runs, patterns, and history across randomizations
source_notes:
Use this when a rule refers to neighbors, runs of bits, or previous transactions. The invariant is to keep rules within one randomization separate from state carried between calls.

**Interview answer.** "Neighbor rules use `foreach` with a guarded index, like `if (i > 0)`. Rules about previous transactions use a non-random class variable that I update in `post_randomize`. I check that any shuffle or post-processing keeps the rules true."

```systemverilog
// Zeros may repeat, but a non-zero value never repeats back to back (Q127).
// Confirm this reading with the interviewer first.
foreach (a[i]) if (i > 0 && a[i] != 0) a[i] != a[i-1];

// Alternate READ and WRITE across calls (Q137)
bit last_was_write;
constraint alt_c { write != last_was_write; }
function void post_randomize(); last_was_write = write; endfunction
```

**Exactly one run of ones in 16 bits (Q124).** Randomize `start` and `len` with `start + len <= 16` and `len >= 1`, then build the value in `post_randomize`. Or use a constraint: the number of positions where bit i is 1 and bit i-1 is 0 (or i is 0) equals 1.

**Symmetric array (Q130).** `foreach (a[i]) a[i] == a[N-1-i];`

**`std::randomize` return value (Q133).** It returns 0 on failure and leaves the variables unchanged. Code that ignores the return value keeps using stale values silently.

**`shuffle()` after constraints (Q142).** `shuffle()` runs after the solver and can break adjacency rules. Either express the order in constraints or re-check after shuffling.

**Stress cases.** A run touching the first or last bit. A cyclic rule (Q140) that must compare the last element with the first. History that resets when a new object is created per transaction.

title: Assertions: immediate vs concurrent, stability, bounded response
source_notes:
Use this to turn a timing rule into an executable check. The invariant is to make the trigger, the delay, the obligation, the sampling clock, and the reset behavior explicit.

**Interview answer.** "An immediate assertion is a procedural check that runs when the statement runs, like an `if`. A concurrent assertion samples signals on a clock in the Preponed region and checks a sequence over time. `|->` checks the consequent in the same cycle, and `|=>` checks it one cycle later. I add a `cover property` for each important assertion so a vacuous pass does not look like success."

```systemverilog
// Payload must stay stable while stalled
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  valid && !ready |=> valid && $stable(payload));

// ack within 1 to MAX_LAT cycles after req rises
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  $rose(req) |-> ##[1:MAX_LAT] ack);
cover property (@(posedge clk) $rose(req) ##[1:MAX_LAT] ack);

// valid stays high until ready (Q148)
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  valid && !ready |=> valid);

// B toggles exactly 2 cycles after A toggles (Q153)
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  $changed(a) |-> ##2 $changed(b));

// cat followed by 3 or 4 dogs (Q149)
assert property (@(posedge clk) cat |=> dog[*3:4] ##1 !dog);
```

**Immediate vs concurrent (Q361).**

```systemverilog
always_comb assert (!(gnt_a && gnt_b)) else $error("double grant"); // immediate
always_comb assert final (!(gnt_a && gnt_b));                       // deferred
```

An immediate assertion can fire on a zero-width glitch while combinational logic settles. A deferred assertion (`assert #0` or `assert final`) reports only the value at the end of the time step. A concurrent assertion is clocked, can span many cycles, and can live in modules, interfaces, and checkers.

**Region order (Q145).** Signals are sampled in Preponed, RTL runs in Active and NBA, assertions are evaluated in Observed, and action blocks run in Reactive. That is why an assertion sees the value from before the clock edge.

**AHB burst must not cross 1KB (Q155).** Check that each SEQ beat stays in the page of the previous beat:

```systemverilog
assert property (@(posedge hclk) disable iff (!hresetn)
  htrans == 2'b11 |-> haddr[31:10] == $past(haddr[31:10]));
```

**Stress cases.** Payload changes during a stall. ack arrives one cycle early or late. Overlapping requests: decide whether each `req` needs its own `ack`. Reset in the middle of an obligation: decide whether `disable iff` should cancel it.

title: Real-time clock and pulse measurement
source_notes:
Use this to check pulse width, duty cycle, period, or jitter. The invariant is to measure elapsed time between the relevant edges, because counting cycles cannot see a glitch shorter than a cycle.

**Interview answer.** "I timestamp edges with `$realtime` and compare the difference with the bound. Same-direction edges give the period, opposite edges give high or low time. I discard the first measurement after reset because it starts from an arbitrary point."

```systemverilog
realtime t_rise, t_fall;
bit have_rise;
always @(posedge sig) begin
  realtime p;
  p = $realtime - t_rise;
  if (have_rise && (p < EXP*0.95 || p > EXP*1.05))   // 5% tolerance (Q150)
    `uvm_error("PERIOD", $sformatf("period %0t", p))
  t_rise = $realtime; have_rise = 1;
end
always @(negedge sig)
  if (have_rise && ($realtime - t_rise) < 2.5ns)
    `uvm_error("GLITCH", "high pulse shorter than 2.5 ns")
```

Keep the parentheses around the two bound checks. Without them, `&&` binds tighter than `||` and the first measurement after reset reports a false error.

**Assertion form (Q147, Q159).**

```systemverilog
property min_high(realtime min_w);
  realtime t;
  @(posedge sig) (1, t = $realtime) |=> @(negedge sig) ($realtime - t) >= min_w;
endproperty
```

Use `|=>` here, because the antecedent and consequent use different clocks.

**Asynchronous change of the expected period (Q151).** Decide which interval uses the old value and which uses the new one, for example by latching the expected period at each measured edge.

**Clock with jitter or random start (Q89, Q239).**

```systemverilog
initial begin
  clk = $urandom_range(0, 1);                 // random initial level
  #($urandom_range(0, 1000) * 1ps);           // random start phase
  forever begin
    int j = int'($urandom_range(0, 2*JIT_PS)) - JIT_PS;  // signed jitter
    #(HALF + j * 1ps) clk = ~clk;
  end
end
```

**Delay of 0 to 1.25 clock periods (Q193).** `#($urandom_range(0, 125) * PERIOD / 100)`, with `timeprecision` fine enough to represent the step.

**Stress cases.** A pulse shorter than the timescale precision, rounding at the exact bound, and a stale expected period.

title: Process ownership, fork/join, and timeouts
source_notes:
Use this to start parallel work with a bounded lifetime and safe cleanup. The invariant is that every spawned process has an owner, a completion condition, and a cleanup rule.

**Interview answer.** "`join` waits for all children, `join_any` for the first, and `join_none` for none. To time out a task, I fork the task and a delay with `join_any`, then `disable fork`. I wrap that in an outer `fork ... join` so `disable fork` kills only these two threads and not unrelated ones started earlier by the same parent."

```systemverilog
fork
  begin
    fork
      do_work();
      begin
        #TIMEOUT;
        `uvm_error("TIMEOUT", "Operation exceeded latency bound")
      end
    join_any
    disable fork;
  end
join
```

**Loop variable capture (Q178, Q197).**

```systemverilog
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) begin
  automatic int k = i;   // each thread gets its own copy
  fork
    run(k);
  join_none
end
wait fork;               // wait for all of them
```

Without `automatic int k`, all three threads see the final value `i == 3`.

**After any two of three tasks (Q180).** Use a counter or a semaphore: each task increments a shared counter when it finishes, and the parent does `wait (done_cnt >= 2)`.

**Disable one branch (Q182, Q190).** Name the block (`begin : b2 ... end`) and call `disable b2;`, or keep a `process` handle from `process::self()` and call `p.kill()`.

**Stress cases.** A killed thread holds a semaphore key or a credit, and `disable fork` does not return it. A task and the timeout finish in the same time step. `wait fork` also waits for threads you did not mean to include.

title: Handles, copying, and polymorphism
source_notes:
Use this to trace shared state, virtual dispatch, casting, and ownership. The invariant is that a handle, the object it points to, and that object's real type are three different things.

**Interview answer.** "A class variable is a handle. Assigning handles shares one object. `copy` or `clone` makes a new object, and nested objects are shared unless `do_copy` copies them too. A `virtual` method dispatches on the object's real type. A non-virtual method dispatches on the handle's declared type. `$cast` checks a downcast at run time and returns 0 on failure."

```systemverilog
class shape;            virtual function real area(); return 0; endfunction endclass
class circle extends shape;
  real r;
  virtual function real area(); return 3.14159*r*r; endfunction
endclass

shape s; circle c = new; c.r = 1;
s = c;                         // upcast, always legal
$display(s.area());            // 3.14159: virtual dispatch uses the real type
if (!$cast(c, s)) $error("not a circle");  // downcast, checked at run time
```

**Method.**

- Draw handles as arrows to objects.

- For each call, ask whether the method is virtual, and which class the object really is.

- Check every `$cast` on a downcast.

- Separate handle assignment, shallow copy, and deep copy.

**Pass by value vs `ref` (Q173).** Passing a handle by value lets the callee modify the object but not make the caller's handle point elsewhere. With `ref`, `h = new` inside the callee changes the caller's handle.

**Abstract class (Q201).** `virtual class` cannot be instantiated. `pure virtual` methods force every subclass to implement them. Use it for a base driver or base sequence that defines an interface.

**Singleton (Q170, Q172).** A static handle, a `protected` constructor, and a static `get()` that creates the object on first use.

**Override vs overload (Q199).** SV supports override (same signature in a subclass), but not overload by argument types as C++ does.

**Component vs object (Q253).** `uvm_component` is static, has a parent and phases, and exists for the whole simulation. `uvm_object` is dynamic data such as items, sequences, and configs.

**Stress cases.** Two queue entries point to one mutable object. A copied object still shares a nested object. A downcast fails. A missing `virtual` keyword breaks expected polymorphism.

title: FSMs and sequence detectors
source_notes:
Use this when outputs depend on recent input history. The invariant is that state holds only the history the future needs. For a pattern detector, state means "the longest suffix of the input so far that is also a prefix of the pattern".

**Interview answer.** "I first ask Mealy or Moore, and overlapping or not. Then I name each state by how much of the pattern matched, build the transition table, and only then write RTL with a state register, next-state logic, and output logic separated. On a mismatch I fall back to the longest matching suffix, not to idle."

**Method.**

1. Name each state by its exact meaning.

2. Build the transition table before RTL.

3. Separate the state register from combinational next-state and output logic.

**Example: overlapping 1101 Mealy detector (Q1).**

| State (matched) | in=0 | in=1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S0 "" | S0 | S1 |
| S1 "1" | S0 | S2 |
| S2 "11" | S3 | S2 |
| S3 "110" | S0 | S1, out=1 |

After a detection on "1101" the last "1" is the start of a new match, so S3 with input 1 goes to S1.

**Serial divisibility by N (Q48).** Track the remainder of the bits seen so far, most significant bit first:

$$
r_{next} = (2r + bit_{in}) \bmod N
$$

For N = 5 that gives five states, one per remainder. If bits arrive least significant first, you also need to track the current power of 2 modulo N.

**Moore vs Mealy (Q202).** Moore output depends only on state and appears one cycle later but is glitch-free. Mealy output depends on input too, reacts in the same cycle, and needs one fewer state. A shift register detector compares the last N bits directly and costs N flops.

**Stress cases.** A mismatch that does not mean idle, overlapping patterns, and an input that ends one match while starting another.

title: FIFO occupancy, boundaries, depth, and verification
source_notes:
Use this to design or check buffering. The invariant is to count accepted pushes and pops, not attempted requests.

**Interview answer.** "Push happens when write is requested and the FIFO is not full, pop when read is requested and it is not empty. Count changes by push minus pop. I check full and empty with simultaneous push and pop, depth 1, and non-power-of-two depth, and I verify against a queue model in the scoreboard."

```text
push = write_request && !full
pop  = read_request  && !empty
next_count = count + push - pop
```

**Widths.** A counter from 0 to DEPTH needs `$clog2(DEPTH + 1)` bits, so depth 5 needs 3 bits. An address pointer needs `$clog2(DEPTH)` bits and explicit wrap when DEPTH is not a power of two.

**Minimum depth (Q84).** Depth must cover the largest backlog: burst length times (1 minus read rate divided by write rate), plus any reader latency. Example: a burst of 80 words written at 100 MHz and read at 50 MHz builds a backlog of 80 x (1 - 50/100) = 40 words.

**Sync vs async vs circular (Q263).** A synchronous FIFO uses one clock and a counter or pointers. An asynchronous FIFO uses two clocks and Gray-coded pointers (Template 26). "Circular" describes the pointer wrap and applies to both.

**FIFO test plan (Q269, Q278).** Reset state, fill to full, write when full, drain to empty, read when empty, simultaneous push and pop at full and at empty, back-to-back and random gaps, data integrity against a queue model, and (for async) different clock ratios and reset of one side.

**Stress cases.** Simultaneous push and pop when full or empty, depth 1, non-power-of-two wrap, and empty flag timing with registered read data (Q64).

title: CDC and asynchronous FIFO architecture
source_notes:
Use this when information crosses between unrelated clocks. The invariant is to choose a mechanism that keeps the information correct, not one that merely moves the bits.

**Interview answer.** "A single stable level goes through a two-flop synchronizer. A pulse from a fast clock needs stretching or a toggle and handshake. A multi-bit value needs a handshake that holds the data stable or an async FIFO. Synchronizing each bit of a bus separately is wrong because bits can land in different cycles. Same frequency with an unknown phase still needs CDC."

| What crosses | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Stable single-bit level | Two- or three-flop synchronizer |
| Pulse, fast to slow | Toggle or stretch plus synchronizer, or req/ack handshake |
| Multi-bit value | Handshake with stable data, or async FIFO |
| Continuous stream | Dual-clock FIFO |

**Async FIFO.** Each side keeps a binary pointer for its memory address and a Gray copy for crossing. The Gray pointer passes through a two-flop synchronizer into the other domain. Full is computed in the write domain, empty in the read domain. Gray code works because only one bit changes per increment, so a pointer sampled mid-change is either the old or the new value.

**Full and empty with N+1-bit Gray pointers.** Empty when the read pointer equals the synchronized write pointer. Full when the top two bits differ and the rest are equal.

**MTBF (Q5, Q58).**

$$
MTBF = \frac{e^{t_r/\tau}}{T_0 \, f_{clk} \, f_{data}}
$$

Adding a flop adds a full cycle of resolution time to t_r, which raises MTBF exponentially.

**Constraints (Q46).** Gray-coded pointer bits need a max-delay constraint so they arrive within one destination period of each other, for example `set_max_delay -datapath_only <dest_period> -from [wptr_gray regs] -to [sync stage 1]`. Also declare the clocks asynchronous with `set_clock_groups -asynchronous` for the other paths.

**Stress cases.** A pulse too short for the receiving clock, events faster than a toggle handshake can carry, independently synchronized bits forming a wrong word, and reset reaching only one side.

title: Setup, hold, clock dividers, and clock-path reasoning
source_notes:
Use this to explain a timing limit or judge a proposed timing fix. The invariant is to draw the launch and capture edges before using any equation.

**Interview answer.** "Setup checks that data launched on one edge arrives before the next capture edge. Hold checks that new data does not arrive too soon after the same edge. Lowering the clock frequency fixes setup but not hold, because the hold check does not depend on the period."

With skew defined as capture clock latency minus launch clock latency:

$$
T_{clk} + T_{skew} \ge T_{cq,max} + T_{comb,max} + T_{setup} + T_{uncertainty}
$$

$$
T_{cq,min} + T_{comb,min} \ge T_{hold} + T_{skew} + T_{uncertainty}
$$

**Fixes.** Setup: shorten logic, pipeline, use faster cells, useful skew, or lower frequency. Hold: add delay cells on the data path. Positive skew helps setup and hurts hold.

**Divide by 3 with 50% duty (Q30).**

```systemverilog
logic [1:0] cnt; logic p, n;
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) cnt <= 0; else cnt <= (cnt == 2) ? 0 : cnt + 1;
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) p <= 0; else p <= (cnt == 0);   // high 1 of 3 cycles
always_ff @(negedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) n <= 0; else n <= p;            // same pulse, half a cycle later
assign clk_div3 = p | n;                      // high for 1.5 of 3 cycles
```

Declare the output with `create_generated_clock` (Q50), for example `create_generated_clock -name clk_div3 -source [get_ports clk] -divide_by 3 [get_pins u_or/Y]`.

**Clock gating (Q78).** A plain AND gate on the clock glitches if enable changes while the clock is high. An integrated clock gate latches enable while the clock is low (a negative-level latch), then ANDs it with the clock, so enable can only change when the AND output is already low.

**Clock mux glitch (Q100).** `sel ? clk1 : clk2` can produce a runt pulse when `sel` changes. The glitch-free mux uses two enable flops, one per clock, each clocked on its own falling edge, with cross-coupled feedback. One clock's enable turns off before the other turns on.

title: RTL coding, resets, and simulation scheduling
source_notes:
Use this to trace cycle values, avoid latches, and explain races. The invariant is to separate evaluation, state update, and observation.

**Interview answer.** "I use nonblocking assignments for flops and blocking assignments for combinational logic. Mixing them, or reading a variable from two processes in the same time step, creates races because the order between processes is not defined. Every combinational block gets default assignments so synthesis does not infer a latch."

**Rules.**

- Give combinational blocks a default assignment and cover every branch, or synthesis infers a latch (Q67).

- Use `<=` for clocked state and `=` for combinational logic.

- `<=` evaluates the right side in Active and updates in NBA. That is why `a <= b; b <= a;` swaps (Q184).

- Rising-edge detector: register the previous value and output `cur && !prev` (Q110, Q174).

**Pipeline trace (Q68, Q85).** With blocking `A = in; B = A; C = B;` in one `always @(posedge clk)`, all three get `in` in the same cycle, which is one register. With `<=`, they form a three-stage shift register.

**Synchronous vs asynchronous reset (Q32).** Synchronous reset needs a running clock, acts only on an edge, and is easy to time. Asynchronous reset works without a clock but must be released synchronously, or flops leave reset in different cycles. The standard fix is a reset synchronizer:

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge arst_n)
  if (!arst_n) {rst_q2, rst_q1} <= 2'b00;
  else         {rst_q2, rst_q1} <= {rst_q1, 1'b1};
assign rst_n_sync = rst_q2;   // asserts immediately, releases on a clock edge
```

**Task vs function (Q162).**

|   | function | task |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consumes time | No | Yes (`#`, `@`, `wait`) |
| Returns | One value, or `void` | Through `output`/`ref` arguments |
| Can call | Functions only (it may start `fork ... join_none`) | Tasks and functions |
| Typical use | Calculations, `write()` callbacks | Driving a bus, waiting for events |

**Streaming operators (Q165).**

```systemverilog
logic [7:0]  u [4] = '{8'h11, 8'h22, 8'h33, 8'h44};
logic [3:0][7:0] p;
logic [31:0] f, r, b;
f = {>>{u}};      // 32'h11223344: u[0] goes to the most significant byte
r = {<<8{f}};     // 32'h44332211: reverse the byte order
b = {<<{f}};      // reverse the bit order
f = p;            // a packed 2D array is already one 32-bit vector
```

**`$display`, `$strobe`, `$monitor`, `$write` (Q163).** `$display` prints immediately with a newline. `$write` prints without a newline. `$strobe` prints at the end of the time step, after NBA updates. `$monitor` prints whenever a listed argument changes.

**`case`, `casez`, `casex` (Q164).** `casez` treats `z` and `?` as don't-care. `casex` also treats `x` as don't-care, which can hide X bugs, so prefer `casez` or `case inside`.

**`timescale 1ns/1ps` (Q76).** Delays are in nanoseconds and rounded to 1 ps, so `#1.23456` becomes 1.235 ns. `timescale` carries across files in compile order, so prefer `timeunit` and `timeprecision` in each module or package.

**Flop with a power check (Q77).** Add a supply-good input and drive `q` to `'x` while supply is off. This is how power-aware simulation shows that state is lost.

title: Datapaths, reductions, and arbitration
source_notes:
Use this to turn arithmetic or arbitration rules into hardware. The invariant is to settle widths, overflow, and selection policy before optimizing structure.

**Interview answer.** "I first decide signedness, result width, and what happens on overflow, saturate or wrap. Then I separate latency from throughput. A balanced tree cuts logic depth from N to log N, and pipelining raises frequency but adds cycles of latency that the testbench must know."

**Method.**

- Decide signedness, extension, overflow, and saturation.

- Separate the latency requirement from the throughput requirement.

- Compare serial, balanced-tree, and pipelined structures.

**Fixed-priority arbiter.** `grant = req & ~(req - 1)` isolates the lowest set bit, so bit 0 has highest priority. Logic depth grows with width. For 128 requesters (Q70), use a tree of 4- or 8-bit priority blocks.

**Locked fixed priority (Q3).** Once a requester wins, keep its grant until it drops its request, even if a higher priority request arrives.

**Round-robin.** Keep a rotating priority pointer and move it past the last winner after each accepted grant.

**Saturating `a*b + c` (Q45).** Compute at full width (2N+1 bits), compare with the max and min of the output type, and clamp.

**Carry-select adder (Q115).** Compute each upper block twice, assuming carry-in 0 and 1, and pick one with the real carry. Delay drops from N full-adder stages to one block plus a chain of muxes, at roughly double the area.

**Sliding window count of ones (Q28).** Keep a running count. Add the entering bit and subtract the leaving bit each cycle, using a shift register of width W.

title: Gate puzzles, number formats, and arithmetic tricks
source_notes:
Use this for short logic puzzles and number-representation questions. The invariant is to write the truth table or the bit format first, then derive.

**Interview answer.** "A 2-to-1 mux computes `s ? i1 : i0`, so tying inputs to constants or to other signals makes any 2-input gate. NAND is universal, and a mux from NAND takes four gates."

**Gates from a 2-to-1 mux, `y = s ? i1 : i0` (Q73, Q101).**

| Gate | s | i1 | i0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NOT a | a | 0 | 1 |
| a AND b | a | b | 0 |
| a OR b | a | 1 | b |
| a XOR b | a | ~b | b |
| a NAND b | a | ~b | 1 (needs a second mux for ~b) |

**2-to-1 mux from NAND only (Q27).** Four gates: `ns = NAND(s,s); t0 = NAND(i0,ns); t1 = NAND(i1,s); y = NAND(t0,t1)`. A 4-to-1 mux takes three 2-to-1 muxes in two levels (Q188). In RTL, write it as a `case` on the select, a nested `?:`, or an indexed vector `y = in[sel]` (Q112).

**Inverter from unknown gates X and Y (Q19).** Write each gate's truth table, then look for a way to tie inputs together or to a constant that leaves a one-input function equal to NOT.

**Two's complement width of A - B (Q29).** Two N-bit signed operands need N+1 bits. For unsigned operands with a possibly negative result, zero-extend both and subtract in N+1 signed bits: `$signed({1'b0,a}) - $signed({1'b0,b})`.

**Gray code (Q2).** Binary to Gray: `g = b ^ (b >> 1)`. Gray to binary: `b[i] = ^g[N-1:i]`. Transition checker:

```systemverilog
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  g != $past(g) |-> $onehot(g ^ $past(g)));
```

**Booth multiplication (Q52).** Radix 2 looks at bits (q0, q-1): 01 adds M, 10 subtracts M, 00 and 11 do nothing, then shift right arithmetically. Radix 4 looks at three bits and selects 0, plus or minus M, or plus or minus 2M, which halves the number of partial products.

**4x4 array multiplier (Q55).** 16 AND gates for partial products. An unsigned N x N array uses N(N-2) full adders and N half adders, so 8 full adders and 4 half adders for N = 4.

**IEEE 754 single precision (Q93).** 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits with bias 127, 23 fraction bits with a hidden leading 1. Exponent 0 means zero or subnormal. Exponent 255 means infinity (fraction 0) or NaN. Default rounding is round to nearest, ties to even. Edge cases to test: +0 equals -0, NaN is not equal to itself, overflow to infinity, underflow to subnormal.

**Fibonacci in RTL (Q20).** Two registers: `a <= b; b <= a + b;`. Size them for the largest term you need, or flag overflow.

**Waveform from NOR plus two flops (Q21).** Write each flop's D input as a function of the current Q outputs, start from the reset values, and fill in a table one clock at a time.

title: Low power, safety, security, and memories
source_notes:
Use this for power-management, UPF, safety, and SRAM questions. The invariant is that every power-down and power-up step has a defined order, and verification must show that no corrupted value leaks out of a domain that is off.

**Interview answer.** "Dynamic power is alpha times C times V squared times f, so lowering voltage helps most. Clock gating cuts switching, multi-Vt and power gating cut leakage. Power gating needs isolation on the outputs of the off domain, retention for state you must keep, and a defined sequence. In power-aware simulation the off domain goes to X, and I check that isolation clamps keep that X from reaching the always-on logic."

$$
P_{dyn} = \alpha \, C \, V^2 f
$$

| Technique | Saves | What to verify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clock gating | Dynamic | No glitches, enable timing, same function with gating on and off |
| Operand isolation | Dynamic | Idle datapath inputs held constant |
| Multi-Vt cells | Leakage | Timing only, no functional change |
| Power gating | Leakage | Isolation clamps, retention save and restore, reset on power-up, no X leakage |
| Multiple voltages | Dynamic | Level shifters on every crossing |
| DVFS | Both | Raise V before f when speeding up; lower f before V when slowing down |

**Typical power-gating order.** Down: stop clocks, enable isolation, save retention, switch off. Up: switch on and wait for stable supply, restore retention, release reset, disable isolation, start clocks.

**UPF sketch (Q97).**

```tcl
create_power_domain PD_CORE -elements {u_core}
create_supply_net VDD_CORE
set_isolation iso_core -domain PD_CORE -applies_to outputs \
    -clamp_value 0 -isolation_signal iso_en -isolation_sense high
set_retention ret_core -domain PD_CORE \
    -save_signal {save high} -restore_signal {restore high}
```

**Safety-aware design (Q11, Q14).** Parity or ECC on storage and buses, duplicated or triplicated logic with voting, watchdogs, and a defined safe state. Lockstep runs two copies of a core, often a couple of cycles apart, and compares outputs every cycle. That roughly doubles core area and power and adds a comparator.

**Security-aware design (Q12).** Lock bits that block writes after boot, no debug backdoors in production, clearing secrets on reset and on mode change, FSMs that recover from illegal states, and constant-time behavior for operations on secrets.

**SRAM (Q49, Q94, Q54).** A single-port SRAM does one read or write per cycle. A dual-port SRAM does two, at more area. SRAM arrays have no reset because adding reset to every bit costs too much area, so software or BIST initializes them, and the testbench must not read before writing. For power, split a large memory into banks and enable only the bank you access, because shorter bitlines cost less energy per access.

title: Bit manipulation and in-place operations
source_notes:
Use this for bit tricks and in-place sequence updates. The invariant is to fix width, signedness, and the loop end condition first.

**Interview answer.** "`x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, so a power of two is a positive number where that gives zero, and popcount is how many times you can do it before reaching zero."

```c
bool is_pow2(unsigned x)   { return x && !(x & (x - 1)); }           // Q331
int  popcount(unsigned x)  { int n = 0; while (x) { x &= x - 1; n++; } return n; }  // Q333
bool bit_set(unsigned x, int n) { return (x >> n) & 1u; }            // Q302
unsigned set_bit(unsigned x, int n)   { return x |  (1u << n); }     // Q87
unsigned clear_bit(unsigned x, int n) { return x & ~(1u << n); }     // Q87
int single(int *a, int n) { int r = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) r ^= a[i]; return r; } // Q303
```

**Reverse 32 bits (Q300).** Loop 32 times: `r = (r << 1) | (x & 1); x >>= 1;`. Or swap halves, then bytes, nibbles, pairs, and single bits with masks.

**Reverse a linked list (Q308).** Three pointers: `prev = NULL; while (cur) { next = cur->next; cur->next = prev; prev = cur; cur = next; } return prev;`

**Move zeros to end (Q327).** A write index copies each non-zero forward, then fills the rest with zeros. This keeps order and runs in O(n).

**`memcpy` safety (Q309).** Overlapping buffers need `memmove`. Check sizes against the destination, not the source. Watch for null pointers and integer overflow in the length.

**Fibonacci (Q329).** Naive recursion is O(2^n). Iteration or memoization is O(n).

**Stress cases.** Zero, shifting by the full width (undefined in C), sign extension on right shift of signed values, and empty lists.

title: Caches, coherence, pipelines, and interrupts
source_notes:
Use this to walk address mapping, cache ownership, or pipeline hazards. The invariant is to state the cache geometry, who owns the latest data, and the ordering model before walking a trace.

**Interview answer.** "I split the address into tag, index, and offset from the cache geometry. For coherence I track each core's line state. In MESI a write needs the line in M or E, so other copies must be invalidated first. MOESI adds O, which lets a dirty line be shared without writing it back to memory first."

For power-of-two line size and set count:

$$
offsetBits = \log_2(lineSize)
$$

$$
indexBits = \log_2(numberOfSets), \quad numberOfSets = \frac{cacheSize}{lineSize \times ways}
$$

$$
tagBits = addressWidth - indexBits - offsetBits
$$

**Worked case (Q113).** 32KB, 4-way, 32-byte lines, 32-bit address: 32768 / (32 x 4) = 256 sets. Offset 5 bits, index 8 bits, tag 19 bits.

**MESI and MOESI (Q23, Q38, Q51).** M: dirty, only copy. E: clean, only copy. S: clean, possibly shared. I: invalid. O (MOESI): dirty but shared, and this cache supplies the data. When two processors write the same line, one wins ownership and the other's copy is invalidated, then the second write takes ownership in turn.

**Hazards (Q6).** RAW is a true dependency, solved by forwarding or a stall. A load followed by a use still stalls one cycle in a classic 5-stage pipeline. WAR and WAW appear only with out-of-order execution and are solved by register renaming.

**Out-of-order (Q35, Q36, Q37).** The reorder buffer commits in program order so exceptions stay precise. The register alias table maps architectural registers to physical ones. A checkpoint (CFC) copy of the table restores it after a mispredicted branch.

**Replacement (Q17).** True LRU over 16 ways needs a full order. Tree PLRU needs 15 bits per set, one per tree node, flipped away from the accessed way.

**Write-back vs write-through (Q24).** Write-back writes memory only on eviction of a dirty line. Write-through writes memory on every store.

**Interrupts (Q90).** An interrupt is an asynchronous signal asking the CPU for service. The CPU finishes the current instruction, saves context, jumps to the handler, the handler clears the source (often a write-1-to-clear bit), and the CPU returns. Ask about level vs edge, masking, and priority.

**Jump immediate vs jump register (Q99).** Jump immediate encodes the target in the instruction. Jump register reads it from a register, which makes function returns and computed jumps possible.

title: Transistor-level circuit analysis
source_notes:
Use this for device operating regions and CMOS networks. The invariant is to decide each transistor's operating region before you apply an equation.

**Interview answer.** "For a CMOS gate, the NMOS network pulls down and the PMOS network pulls up, and they are duals. A NAND has NMOS in series because the output goes low only when all inputs are high, and PMOS in parallel because any low input pulls it high. Series NMOS are made wider to keep pull-down strength equal to the inverter."

**Method.**

1. Find Vgs and Vds for each device.

2. Check threshold voltage and body effect.

3. Analyze pull-up and pull-down paths, switching threshold, and noise margins.

4. Add parasitic capacitance, charge sharing, and leakage where they matter.

**NAND2 sizing (Q350).** If the reference inverter has NMOS width 1 and PMOS width 2, a NAND2 uses NMOS width 2 each (two in series) and PMOS width 2 each (in parallel, worst case one on).

**Latch-up (Q56).** A parasitic PNPN thyristor between the wells turns on and shorts supply to ground. Prevent it with well taps, guard rings, and spacing.

**Electromigration (Q355).** Black's equation gives mean time to failure `MTTF = A * J^-n * exp(Ea/kT)`. Use average current for DC wear-out and RMS current for self-heating.

**RC low-pass filter (Q26, Q356).**

$$
H(s) = \frac{1}{1 + sRC}, \qquad f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}
$$

At f_c the gain is -3 dB and the phase is -45 degrees. Above f_c the gain falls 20 dB per decade. The step response is `V(1 - e^(-t/RC))`. Example: R = 1 kOhm and C = 1 uF give f_c of about 159 Hz.

**Stress cases.** A device you assumed saturated is in the linear region. Charge sharing changes a dynamic node. Leakage breaks an ideal static assumption.

title: What is a UVM RAL model? Why is it required?
source_notes: RAL is short for Register Abstraction Layer. It is a set of base classes that can be used to create register models to mimic the register contents in a design. It is much easier to write and read from the design using a register model than sending a bus transaction for every read and write. Also the register model stores the current state of the design in a local copy called as a *mirrored* value. Read more in [Register Layer](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-register-layer).

title: What is p_sequencer, and where is it used?
source_notes: `p_sequencer` is a handle to the sequencer on which the current sequence should be executed and is made available in a sequence by the macro `` `uvm_declare_p_sequencer ``. It is typically accessed within sequences to start other sequences.

title: What is the difference between new() and create()?
source_notes: The `new()` method is the classical way of how SV creates an object instance. The `create()` is an addition in UVM that allows the factory to return an object of the type that we want. Read more in [Using factory overrides](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-factory-override).

title: Is UVM independent of SystemVerilog?
source_notes: No. UVM is built on SystemVerilog and hence you cannot run UVM with any tool that does not support SystemVerilog.

title: Why do we need to register a class with a factory?
source_notes: You don't necessarily need to. It is registered with a factory simply to make the testbench more re-usable and have the capability to override it with some other derivative component later on. Read more in [Using factory overrides](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-factory-override).

title: What are Active and Passive modes in an agent?
source_notes:
An *agent* typically consists of a driver, sequencer and a monitor. At times, we don't want the agent to drive anything to the DUT but simply monitor the signals on the interface. This is a passive agent where sequencer and driver are not instantiated at all. An active agent is when it can run sequences on its sequencer, drive signals and monitor the interface.

Read more on [UVM Agent](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-agent).

title: What is a TLM Fifo?
source_notes: When two components at different clocks need to be operating independently, you have to insert a TLM FIFO in between. One component can send data at a faster rate while the other component can receive at a slower rate. Read more in [TLM Fifo](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-tlm-fifo)

title: What are the advantages of `uvm_component_utils and `uvm_object_utils?
source_notes: These macros are used to register a class with the factory. `` `uvm_component_utils `` is used when the class is a *component* derived from `uvm_component`, and `` `uvm_object_utils `` is used if it's an object derived from `uvm_object`. There are no advantages from one over the other but are separate ways to register with the factory. Read more in [Using factory overrides](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-factory-override).

title: How does a sequence start?
source_notes: A sequence can be started by calling its `start()` method or by using the macro `` `uvm_do ``. Read more in [Executing sequences via start()](https://chipverify.com/uvm/how-to-execute-sequences-via-start-method) and [Executing sequences via macros](https://chipverify.com/uvm/how-to-execute-sequences-via-uvm-do-macros)

title: How can we access a DUT signal in a component or sequence?
What is RALGEN and how do you use it?
source_notes:
RALGEN is a Synopsys tool to generate RAL model from an IPXACT specification file. You simply have to specify a few options and select the block for which you need to generate class structure for and provide them to the tool.

Read more about [register model](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-register-model) !

title: What are desired and mirrored values in RAL?
source_notes:
Desired values are those that we want the design to have, and can later update the design with. Mirrored values are those that reflect the latest known values in the DUT.

Read more about [desired and mirrored values](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-register-model) !

title: What are reg2bus and bus2reg functions for?
source_notes: They are RAL functions that enable conversion from generic register contents to actual bus transactions and vice-versa. You have to define them based on the protocol you are dealing with by assigning the data object of the protocol with values from `rw` internal variable and vice-versa.

title: How would you debug a config db name or path mismatch problem?
source_notes: You can use the command-line define `+UVM_CONFIG_DB_TRACE` to dump information related to all SET and GET calls done on the configuration DB. It also shows you the path, and instance that makes the call.

title: What are the different TB components in UVM?
source_notes:
Some of the major components are driver, monitor, scoreboard, sequencer, agent, environment, test and sequences.

Read more on [UVM Introduction](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-introduction).

title: Which UVM phase takes more time and why?
source_notes: Run time phases take more time because they are the major phases that consume simulation time. The times taken for each test can be different because they all test different aspects of a design.

title: How do you connect a monitor with a scoreboard?
source_notes: You can declare the implementation of an analysis port within a scoreboard and connect the monitor's analysis port with it in the environment's connect method.

title: How do you connect driver and sequencer?
source_notes: Driver has a TLM port called `seq_item_port` that can be connected with the sequencer's `seq_item_export` in an agent's connect method.

title: What is uvm_config_db and uvm_resource_db?
source_notes: Both are mechanisms that allow a component to place an object in a central look-up table under a specified *name* and *path*, so that they can be retrieved by another component using the same *name* and *path*. The `uvm_config_db` class provides a convenience interface on top of the `uvm_resource_db` to simplify the basic interface that is used for configuring `uvm_component` instances.

title: What are the different phases in UVM?
source_notes:
The main phases in UVM are :

- build_phase

- connect_phase

- end_of_elaboration_phase

- start_of_simulation_phase

- run_phase

- extract_phase

- check_phase

- report_phase

- final_phase

Read more in [UVM Phases](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-phases).

title: What is a virtual sequence and a virtual sequencer?
source_notes: A virtual sequence is a container to hold and execute multiple other smaller sequences. A virtual sequencer is a container to hold the handles to other sequencers in an environment so that each sequence in a virtual sequence can be executed on the appropriate sequencer. Read more in [Virtual Sequence](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-virtual-sequence) and [Virtual Sequencer](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-virtual-sequencer)

title: What is the difference between `uvm_do and `uvm_send?
source_notes: `` `uvm_do `` macro will automatically create a new object, randomize it and send to the the sequencer. `` `uvm_send `` is used when the object is already created and randomized but needs to be executed on a sequencer. Read more in [How to execute sequences via `uvm_do macros ?](https://chipverify.com/uvm/how-to-execute-sequences-via-uvm-do-macros) and [Sequence action macros for pre-existing items](https://chipverify.com/uvm/sequence-action-macros-for-pre-existing-items)

title: What is the difference between uvm_transaction and uvm_sequence_item?
source_notes: The `uvm_transaction` class is the root base class for UVM transactions and has a timing and recording interface as well. Use of this class as a base for user-defined transactions is deprecated, and instead its sub-class `uvm_sequence_item` should be used. The intended use of transaction API is to call `accept_tr`, `begin_tr` and `end_tr` during the course of sequence item execution in order to record the events to a vendor-specific transaction database. `uvm_sequence_item` is primarily used to define data objects and related methods.

title: What are the benefits of using UVM?
source_notes:
Some of the major and immediate benefits are :

- Testbench prototyping becomes faster because of all the base classes for drivers, monitors, sequencers

- There's a well defined reporting system which supports various levels of verbosities like LOW, DEBUG, etc

- Supports register model creation and maintainence which simplifies the way DUT registers are accessed

- Well structured plug and play style components like agents that can be plugged into any environment to support a particular protocol

- Factory helps to override certain components without having to modify existing connections in the testbench

- Configuration databases that allow components to share objects and data between each other

- Make use of TLM features that enable different components that receive transactions to perform different operations on it.

- Promotes re-usability, flexibility, uniformity and robustness to every testbench built on UVM

title: Is it possible to have a user defined phase in UVM?
source_notes:
Yes, you can define your own phase and insert it between any of the existing phases. For this, you have to first define a new phase class inherited from `uvm_task_phase`, implement the `exec_task` or `exec_func` method and insert the phase into existing schedule or domain object.

Read more on [Creating user-defined phases](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-user-defined-phase).

title: What is the difference between RAL backdoor and frontdoor accesses?
source_notes: A backdoor access in RAL is a way to dump values directly onto the DUT registers via a hard coded RTL signal path and does not consume simulation time. A frontdoor access in RAL is usually done by sending the data as a transaction through an associated peripheral bus interface and hence consumes simulation time.

title: What is a phase objection?
source_notes: In UVM, all components synchronize with each other through a set of phases. Every component has to finish its processes in a particular phase until it can proceed to the next. So, objection is a mechanism to allow a component to stall other components from proceeding to the next phase until it gets the chance to finish its own tasks. This is normally done using `raise_objection()` and `drop_objection()` methods from the `uvm_phase` class.

title: What is the difference between set_config_ and uvm_config_db*?
source_notes:
The basic `set_config_*` methods are mapped to corresponding `uvm_config_db` as :

```systemverilog
set_config_int(...) => uvm_config_db#(uvm_bitstream_t)::set(cntxt,...)
set_config_string(...) => uvm_config_db#(string)::set(cntxt,...)
set_config_object(...) => uvm_config_db#(uvm_object)::set(cntxt,...)
```

title: What are the different factory override types?
source_notes:
Factory overrides can be done in four different ways:

- Instance override by type of the component/object

- Instance override by name of the component/object

- Type override by type of the component/object

- Type override by name of the component/object

Note that calling `create()` with a single argument omits the context needed for an instance override for an object. To provide this context, you can either pass this as the second argument to use the current component's path, or supply a third argument to define an explicit absolute path string.

Read more on [UVM Factory Override](https://chipverify.com/uvm/uvm-factory-override).

What does a sequence normally contain?
source_notes:
A sequence has a task called `body()` within which we can write the actual stimulus to test the design for a particular feature.
